Satellites, constellations and orbits¶

These three modules build and propagate the satellites. An Orbit_specification holds the orbital elements; a Satellite turns them (or a TLE) into a propagatable object; a SatelliteConstellation groups satellites and propagates them together. The same constellation class is used for both the LEO receiver fleet and the GNSS transmitter fleets.

A LEO receiver constellation (two near-polar planes at 99.1° inclination and 7300 km semi-major axis, ascending nodes 90° apart).

Orbit specification¶

Summary¶

Orbit_specification is a plain container of six osculating classical orbital elements at an epoch (Table 6). From the semi-major axis \(a\) it derives the mean motion (revolutions per day),

(34)¶\[n = \frac{T_\mathrm{day}}{2\pi\sqrt{a^3 / \mu_\oplus}},\]

with the seconds-per-day \(T_\mathrm{day}\) and Earth’s gravitational parameter \(\mu_\oplus\). The epoch is stored in the TLE YYDDD.DDDDDDDD format, ready for TLE generation.

Satellite¶

Summary¶

The object Satellite is a wrapper around a Skyfield EarthSatellite. It can either be initialised from an Orbit_specification (SGP4 mean elements are fitted and a TLE is generated; see TLE generation) or directly from a TLE file. Once the constellation sets the shared timescale, the propagate methods fill the ECI position and velocity arrays which downstream objects read.

Satellite constellation¶

Summary¶

SatelliteConstellation groups satellites and runs them on one clock. set_simulation_duration builds the Skyfield timescale from a start time, a duration (hours), and a step (seconds), and pushes it down to every satellite; propagate_constellation then propagates them all. The dictionary {"GPS": SatelliteConstellation, ...} returned by the GNSS loader is what the reflection and detection code consumes.

class object_definitions.SatConstellation_def.SatelliteConstellation(satArray=None, tle_file=None, satConfigName=None, rx_antenna=None, verbose=False)[source]¶

A group of satellites propagated together; the same class for the LEO Rx and GNSS Tx fleets.

Initialise with either a list of Satellite objects or a TLE file (not both). set_simulation_duration builds the shared Skyfield timescale and pushes it to every satellite, after which propagate_constellation fills each satellite’s ECI state.

Classical elements to a TLE¶

The receiver orbits in [ORBITS] are osculating classical elements – an instantaneous two-body state. A TLE instead stores SGP4 mean elements: quantities defined through SGP4’s averaged theory, not a snapshot of the Keplerian state. The two differ by the short- and long-period terms SGP4 folds in, so the osculating elements cannot simply be copied into the TLE fields. generate_tle_data_string() therefore fits the mean elements, in three steps.

1. Osculating state at the epoch. The classical elements are turned into an inertial Cartesian state \((\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v})\). In the perifocal frame, with semi-latus rectum \(p = a(1-e^2)\) and true anomaly \(f\),

(35)¶\[\begin{split}r = \frac{p}{1 + e\cos f}, \qquad \mathbf{r}_\mathrm{pf} = r\begin{pmatrix}\cos f\\ \sin f\\ 0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{pf} = \sqrt{\tfrac{\mu_\oplus}{p}}\begin{pmatrix}-\sin f\\ e+\cos f\\ 0\end{pmatrix},\end{split}\]

rotated into the inertial frame by the 3-1-3 sequence of the right ascension of the ascending node \(\Omega\), the inclination \(i\), and the argument of periapsis \(\omega\), \(\mathbf{r} = R_3(\Omega)\,R_1(i)\,R_3(\omega)\,\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{pf}\) (and likewise for \(\mathbf{v}\)). This is the target state the TLE must reproduce.

2. Fit the mean elements. SGP4 mean elements \((a, e, i, \Omega, \omega, M)\) are chosen so that propagating them with SGP4 back to the same epoch returns the target state. A least-squares solver (scipy.optimize.least_squares()) minimises the scaled position/velocity residual

(36)¶\[\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{x}) = \left[\frac{\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{SGP4}(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{r}_\mathrm{target}}{100\ \mathrm{m}},\; \frac{\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{SGP4}(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{target}}{0.1\ \mathrm{m/s}}\right],\]

where \(\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{SGP4}(\mathbf{x})\) is the Skyfield/SGP4 epoch state built from the trial mean elements. The two normalization weights (shown here as the representative \(100\ \mathrm{m}\) and \(0.1\ \mathrm{m/s}\)) make the position and velocity blocks dimensionless and comparable, setting their relative weighting in the fit; they are engine settings read strictly from simulator_settings.yaml (the tle_fit section), not fixed constants. The solver variables \(\mathbf{x}\) are equinoctial-style (\(a,\ i,\ \Omega,\ e\cos\omega,\ e\sin\omega,\ \omega + M\)) to stay well-conditioned as \(e \to 0\) (where \(\omega\) becomes undefined); the osculating elements seed the initial guess. The mean anomaly \(M\) is obtained from the true anomaly \(f\) through the eccentric anomaly \(E\):

(37)¶\[\tan\frac{E}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{1-e}{1+e}}\,\tan\frac{f}{2}, \qquad M = E - e\sin E,\]

the second relation being Kepler’s equation. The implementation evaluates the half-angle relation in the quadrant-safe two-argument form \(E = 2\,\mathrm{arctan2}\!\left(\sqrt{1-e}\,\sin\tfrac{f}{2},\ \sqrt{1+e}\,\cos\tfrac{f}{2}\right)\), which is valid for all quadrants of \(f\). Non-convergence of the least-squares fit emits a warning rather than raising.

3. Write the TLE. The fitted mean elements are formatted onto the two 69-character lines: inclination \(i\), node \(\Omega\), eccentricity \(e\) (\(\times 10^7\)), argument of periapsis \(\omega\) and mean anomaly \(M\) in degrees, and the mean motion \(n = \sqrt{\mu_\oplus/a^3}\) in revolutions per day, alongside the epoch, drag terms and checksums. For a near-circular LEO the result reproduces the requested position to a few metres; the floor comes from TLE field quantisation (angles stored to \(10^{-4}\) deg), not the solver.

Note

Reading a TLE runs the inverse anomaly step. A file stores the mean anomaly \(M\), so read_tle_data() and Satellite convert it to the true anomaly \(f\) (mean_to_true_anomaly_deg()): Kepler’s equation \(M = E - e\sin E\) is solved for \(E\) by Newton iteration, then \(f = 2\,\mathrm{arctan2}\!\left(\sqrt{1+e}\,\sin\tfrac{E}{2},\ \sqrt{1-e}\,\cos\tfrac{E}{2}\right)\) inverts (37). The result is stored in an Orbit_specification – so that container always holds a true anomaly regardless of source. A read TLE’s mean elements are then held as if osculating; this is an accepted approximation because GNSS transmitters are propagated straight from their own TLE, never re-generated.

The ReadWriteSatData API (generate_tle_data_string, read_tle_data, mean_to_true_anomaly_deg) is documented on the Support modules (constants, satellite data I/O, plotting) page.

Module Assumptions and Limitations¶

  • SGP4 / TLE propagation. Motion comes from Skyfield’s SGP4 over a TLE. Auto-generated TLEs have no drag term (B*), so long-window propagation drifts from a real decaying orbit.

  • Osculating-to-mean conversion. User elements describe an instantaneous two-body osculating state. TLE fields are SGP4 mean elements, so generation performs a nonlinear fit whose epoch state matches the requested position and velocity before TLE field quantisation. The numbers written into the TLE should not be interpreted as the original osculating elements.

  • Frame-conversion data. Reflection geometry uses Astropy/PyMap3D ECI/ECEF transforms. Offline runs can use the installed astropy-iers-data table even after its predictive validity window; this avoids a hard failure but degrades Earth-orientation accuracy. Refresh that package/IERS data for precision studies.

  • Either elements or a TLE. A Satellite cannot take both; a constellation cannot take both a satellite list and a TLE file.

  • Duration in hours, step in seconds. set_simulation_duration mixes units by design; the step must be an integer number of seconds.

  • Epoch needed for propagation. Without an epoch on the Orbit_specification the Skyfield object is not built.

User Guide¶

Orbits come from the [ORBITS] INI section, one key per satellite (orbit1 = [inclination_deg, eccentricity, raan_deg, argPeriapsis_deg, trueAnomaly_deg, semiMajorAxis_m]), read in order until the next is missing. The GNSS transmitter constellations are loaded from the TLE files listed in [GNSS CONSTELLATIONS].gnss_tle_files.

from object_definitions.SatConstellation_def import SatelliteConstellation
from object_definitions.Satellite_def import Satellite

sats = [Satellite(i, orbit_n=orbit_list[i]) for i in range(n)]
leo = SatelliteConstellation(satArray=sats, satConfigName="LEO")
leo.set_simulation_duration(start_time, duration_hours, step_seconds)
leo.propagate_constellation(start_time, duration_seconds, step_seconds)

Two-Line Element Sets (TLEs)¶

A Two-Line Element (TLE) is the standard NORAD text format that encodes a satellite’s mean Keplerian elements, epoch, and drag term on two 69-character lines. Every satellite is propagated from a TLE with SGP4 (via Skyfield), so both transmitter (GNSS) and receiver (GNSS-R) satellites run from TLEs:

  • GNSS transmitters are loaded directly from the TLE files listed in [GNSS CONSTELLATIONS].gnss_tle_files and stored under DATA/TLE_EPHEMIRIS/. One file becomes one SatelliteConstellation. The constellation is identified from the file name, which must contain one of GPS, GLONASS, GALILEO, or BEIDOU (case-insensitive); a name that matches none raises.

  • GNSS-R receivers are built from the osculating [ORBITS] elements. The generator fits SGP4 mean elements at the configured epoch and writes a per-satellite TLE under DATA/TLE_EPHEMIRIS/autogenerated/ (git-ignored). Re-generating the same satellite overwrites that satellite’s deterministic autogenerated filename.

For example, the GPS satellite PRN 13 – a name line followed by the two element lines, with the epoch field (25135.33377744) in the YYDDD.DDDDDDDD form noted above:

GPS BIIR-2  (PRN 13)
1 24876U 97035A   25135.33377744  .00000044  00000+0  00000+0 0  9991
2 24876  55.7964 114.1388 0089709  53.8017 306.9996  2.00562545203970

TLE epochs age, and SGP4 accuracy degrades as the propagation window moves away from the epoch, so the GNSS files should be refreshed periodically.

The GNSS TLE files come from CelesTrak.

Each TLE download shall be saved under DATA/TLE_EPHEMIRIS/ with a name that contains the constellation keyword (for example GPS_operational.tle), then list it in [GNSS CONSTELLATIONS].gnss_tle_files.
